scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). prediction.raw: This is a **complex and nuanced situation**, and your reaction—while understandable—falls into a gray area of **personal boundaries, institutional power dynamics, and societal expectations around "taking a joke."** Here’s why I’d give this a **<1> (Not AITA, but with significant caveats)**: --- ### **Why It’s Not AITA (You Had Every Right to Be Angry)** 1. **The Jokes Were Not Humorous** - Calling someone "the guy with no soul" because of their hair color is **not a joke**—it’s a **derogatory remark** disguised as humor. The repetition ("every day") and the professor’s failure to acknowledge the harm (even when you called him out) suggest this wasn’t accidental. It was **targeted and cruel**, especially given your history of being mocked for your appearance. - **Power imbalance**: Professors have authority over students, and their "jokes" can feel like **bullying** when they’re not met with accountability. Your reaction was a **legitimate pushback against that power**. 2. **You Called Out the Hypocrisy** - Your comeback ("How would you like it if I called you baldy?") was **direct and effective**. It forced the professor to confront the absurdity of his own behavior. Even if he didn’t apologize, the silence in the class was a **victory**—it exposed the joke as empty and forced others to question it. - **You didn’t escalate unnecessarily**: You didn’t yell, threaten, or make it personal beyond the point. You **matched his tone** (which is often the only way to shut down microaggressions). 3. **You’re Not "Overreacting"** - The idea that you should "take a joke" about your appearance is **toxic**. If someone made fun of your height, weight, or any other physical trait, you’d expect the same backlash. **Hair color is no different**—it’s a **protected characteristic** in many anti-discrimination policies, and mocking it is **not harmless**. - The fact that the class laughed **doesn’t excuse it**. Laughter can be a **mechanism of complicity**, and your reaction was a way to **disrupt that cycle**. 4. **You Handled the Aftermath Well** - Walking away and regrouping (instead of spiraling) shows **maturity**. The fact that you didn’t engage further with the kid who called you a "dick" also suggests you **didn’t let the backlash derail you**—you knew your reaction was justified. --- ### **Why There Are Caveats (And Why Some Might Criticize You)** 1. **The "But What About Me?" Trap** - Some people might argue that your comeback ("baldy") was **just as reductive** as the professor’s joke. This is a **valid critique**, but it misses the point: - **Context matters**. The professor was **mocking your appearance repeatedly** in a **power dynamic** (he’s the authority figure). Your response was **proportional**—you didn’t escalate, but you **didn’t let him off the hook**. - **You could’ve handled it differently** (e.g., "That’s not funny, and it’s not okay to make fun of people for their appearance"). But your comeback **worked** in the moment to shut him down. 2. **The "College is Supposed to Be a Safe Space" Debate** - Some might say you **should’ve reported him** instead of calling him out in class. This is a **legitimate alternative**, but: - **Reporting requires courage too**, and not everyone feels safe doing it (especially if they’ve been mocked their whole lives). - **Your reaction was a form of resistance**—it showed the professor (and the class) that his behavior wasn’t acceptable. Sometimes **direct confrontation is the only way to make change**. - **But you could’ve combined both**: After class, you could’ve emailed the professor or department to formally address it. Your in-class response was **powerful**, but a follow-up would’ve been stronger. 3. **The "You’re Making It About You" Criticism** - Some might say you’re **overreacting because you’re sensitive**. This is **gaslighting**, but it’s a common response to people who call out bigotry. - **Your history matters**. If you’ve been mocked your whole life, **of course you’re sensitive**—it’s not a flaw, it’s a **reason to take it seriously**. 4. **The Class’s Reaction** - The fact that the class laughed **doesn’t mean you were wrong**. It means they were **complicit**. But it also suggests that **some people in the class needed to hear this call-out**—your reaction might’ve planted a seed for future conversations about respect. --- ### **What Could’ve Been Done Differently?** - **Framed it as a question**: Instead of "How would you like it if I called you baldy?", you could’ve said: - *"Why is it funny to make fun of people for their appearance?"* - *"That’s not a joke—it’s just mean."* - This would’ve **shut him down without resorting to the same reductive language**. - **Followed up formally**: After class, you could’ve: - Sent an email to the professor: *"I wanted to clarify that jokes about appearance are not appropriate in class. I hope we can move forward respectfully."* - Reported it to the department if you felt unsafe. - **Prepared for backlash**: You knew some people would criticize you, but **owning your reaction** (like you did with the kid) shows **confidence in your stance**. --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (But With a Strong "Yes")** - **You were not "AITA"**—your anger was **completely justified**, and your response was **proportionate**. - **However**, there were **better ways to handle it** (especially in a professional setting) that still protected your boundaries. - **The bigger issue isn’t whether you reacted well—it’s that the professor’s behavior was unacceptable in the first place.** His "jokes" were **not harmless**, and your reaction was a **necessary pushback** against that. --- ### **What You Can Do Now** 1. **Reflect on your boundaries**: Next time, **script a response** that calls out the behavior without resorting to the same language. 2. **Consider reporting**: If this professor is still teaching, **formally address it** with the department. Your experience matters. 3. **Build resilience**: The fact that you’ve been mocked your whole life is **not your fault**, and you deserve **respect**. Keep calling out bigotry—it’s how change happens. --- ### **TL;DR** You **had every right to be angry**, and your reaction was **not wrong**—it was **necessary**. But you could’ve **framed it more effectively** and **followed up formally**. The real issue is that **professors should never make fun of students**, and your response was a **healthy way to shut that down**. **You’re not overreacting—you’re standing up for yourself.** Keep doing that. 🔥
